```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(QAST.cores = 2)
```

## Quality-adjusted survival

Survival time alone treats every month of life the same. In many studies,
especially in oncology, the time a patient spends with treatment toxicity or
after a relapse is worth less than time in good health. **Quality-adjusted
survival** weights each period of life by a utility between 0 and 1, so the
quality-adjusted time `qt` of a subject is never larger than the survival
time `t`.

Censoring is harder here than in ordinary survival analysis: subjects with a
poor quality of life accumulate quality-adjusted time slowly, so censoring
becomes informative on that scale. QAST handles this with inverse
probability of censoring weights (IPCW), estimated by Kaplan-Meier or by a
Cox model.

QAST fits **bivariate semiparametric accelerated failure time (AFT)
models** for `t` and `qt` jointly:

* `semi_aft_fg()`: the model of Fine and Gelber (2001), for binary
  covariates, with truncation at a time `L`;
* `semi_aft_prop()`: the model proposed in the doctoral thesis of da Silva
  (2026), for continuous or discrete covariates.

Each fit has two components: `beta` for the survival time and `theta` for
the quality-adjusted survival time.

## Data

Each subject contributes an observed time `t`, a quality-adjusted time `qt`
(with `0 <= qt <= t`), an event indicator `status` (1 = event, 0 =
censored) and covariates. We simulate a small study:

```{r data}
library(QAST)

set.seed(2026)
n <- 150
d <- data.frame(
  trt = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  sex = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 60, 8))
)
t_event <- rexp(n, rate = exp(-0.4 * d$trt))   # treatment lengthens survival
t_cens  <- rexp(n, rate = 0.3)
d$status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens)
d$t  <- pmin(t_event, t_cens)
d$qt <- d$t * runif(n, 0.5, 1)                  # utility between 0.5 and 1
head(d)
```

The response is written with `Qsurv(time, qtime, status)` on the left-hand
side of a formula, like `survival::Surv()`. The models do not estimate an
intercept (their estimating equations are invariant to shifts), and factors
enter as indicators.

## Fine and Gelber model

The Fine and Gelber model needs binary covariates and a truncation time `L`,
usually a time with enough follow-up left, such as an upper quantile of the
observed times:

```{r fg}
fit_fg <- semi_aft_fg(Qsurv(t, qt, status) ~ trt + sex, data = d,
                      L = quantile(d$t, 0.9), var_comp = TRUE)
fit_fg
```

`summary()` adds the jackknife standard errors, z statistics and p-values
for both components:

```{r fg-summary}
summary(fit_fg)
```

On the log scale (`h1 = h2 = "log"`, the defaults), `exp(coef)` is a **time
ratio**: values above 1 mean longer times. Here the treatment lengthens
both the survival time and the quality-adjusted survival time.

The model assumes that the censoring depends on the covariates only through
a discrete partition chosen by the analyst, and weights each subject by the
Kaplan-Meier censoring survival of its group. As in the application of Fine
and Gelber (2001), the default does not stratify. If the censoring depends
on a covariate (which a Cox model of the censoring can show, as in the
article), `cens_group` stratifies by it:

```{r fg-cens}
fit_fg1 <- semi_aft_fg(Qsurv(t, qt, status) ~ trt + sex, data = d,
                       L = quantile(d$t, 0.9), cens_group = d$trt)
coef(fit_fg1)
```

## Proposed model

`semi_aft_prop()` accepts continuous covariates:

```{r prop}
fit_prop <- semi_aft_prop(Qsurv(t, qt, status) ~ age + trt, data = d,
                          var_comp = TRUE)
coef(fit_prop)
vcov(fit_prop, "theta")
```

`coef()` returns a matrix with the `beta` and `theta` columns; `vcov()`
returns the covariance matrix of one component.

## Intercepts

The rank-based estimating equations do not change when every residual is
shifted by the same constant, so they do not identify an intercept. Each
fit estimates it afterwards as the mean of the distribution of the
residuals of its component:

* survival time: the mean of the Kaplan-Meier curve of
  $h_1(T_i) - Z_i^\top\hat\beta$ (Ding and Nan, 2015);
* quality-adjusted time: the IPCW mean
  $n^{-1}\sum_i \delta_i r_i / \hat G(T_i)$ of
  $r_i = h_2(Q_i) - Z_i^\top\hat\theta$ (Zhao and Tsiatis, 2000), the
  mean of the distribution estimated by `surv_qt_fun()`.

```{r intercept}
fit_prop$intercept
# Predicted log survival time and log quality-adjusted time
z <- model.matrix(~ age + trt, d)[, -1]
head(cbind(
  log_t  = fit_prop$intercept[["beta"]]  + drop(z %*% fit_prop$beta),
  log_qt = fit_prop$intercept[["theta"]] + drop(z %*% fit_prop$theta)
))
```

The intercepts have no standard errors and are not part of `coef()` or
`vcov()`.

## Predictions

`predict()` returns the linear predictors (`type = "lp"`, intercept
included) or the survival probabilities given the covariates
(`type = "survival"`). Since the error does not depend on the covariates,
$S(t \mid z) = S_e\{h(t) - z^\top\hat\beta\}$: the Kaplan-Meier curve of the
residuals for the survival time and the Zhao and Tsiatis (1997) estimator
of the residuals for the quality-adjusted time.

```{r predict, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
new <- data.frame(age = c(0, 0), trt = c(0, 1))
predict(fit_prop, new)
tg <- seq(0.1, 3, length.out = 60)
s <- predict(fit_prop, new, type = "survival", times = tg)
matplot(tg, t(s$theta), type = "s", lty = 1:2, col = 1, ylim = c(0, 1),
        xlab = "Quality-adjusted survival time",
        ylab = "Estimated survival probability")
legend("topright", c("trt = 0", "trt = 1"), lty = 1:2, bty = "n")
```

`type = "rmean"` gives the mean time restricted to `tau`,
$E\{\min(T, \tau) \mid z\} = \int_0^\tau S(t \mid z)\,dt$, computed exactly
on the step curves. The restriction avoids the right tail of the curves,
which is not identified when the largest times are censored:

```{r rmean}
predict(fit_prop, new, type = "rmean", tau = 2)
```

## Predictive performance

`qast_metrics()` measures how well the predicted curves fit the observed
data: the Brier score over time, the integrated Brier score, the explained
variation against the model without covariates and the mean absolute error
of the restricted mean. The usual tools treat `(qtime, status)` as
right-censored data and weight by the censoring curve of the
quality-adjusted time, which is biased because that censoring is induced
informative. `qast_metrics()` weights every subject by the censoring
survival on the survival time scale, as the estimator of Zhao and Tsiatis
(1997). It accepts a fit, or a matrix of survival probabilities from any
model, so different models are compared on the same scale:

```{r metrics}
train <- d[1:100, ]
test <- d[101:150, ]
fit_tr <- semi_aft_prop(Qsurv(t, qt, status) ~ age + trt, data = train)
m <- qast_metrics(fit_tr, newdata = test,
                  y = with(test, Qsurv(t, qt, status)))
m
```

A negative explained variation means that the model predicts the test data
worse than the curve without covariates, as can happen with weak effects
and a small test sample. `m$theta$brier` has the Brier score at each time,
and `ipcw_mass`, close to 1, checks that the follow-up covers the survival
times (see `?qast_metrics`).

## Model checking

`qast_pp()` draws the P-P plots of the residuals of Fine and Gelber (2001,
Section 4). Under the model the distribution of the residuals does not
depend on the covariates, so the distributions estimated in two covariate
groups should lie close to the diagonal. Check the survival time component
(a) first: the quality-adjusted diagnostic (b) assumes it is correct. In the
Fine and Gelber model, (b) is the conditional distribution of the
quality-adjusted residuals given the trimming required by the estimating
function of $\theta$. Continuous covariates are discretized to form the
groups:

```{r pp, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6}
pp <- qast_pp(fit_prop, group = cut(d$age, c(-Inf, median(d$age), Inf),
                                    labels = c("younger", "older")))
pp
plot(pp)
```

## Variance

Standard errors come from the delete-1 jackknife (`var_method =
"jackknife"`, the default) or the bootstrap (`var_method = "bootstrap"`,
with `M` resamples of the subjects). Each replicate refits the whole
estimator, beta, the censoring weights and theta, on the same subsample or
resample; replicates in which a covariate loses rank are discarded, with a
warning. The replicates run in parallel on the physical cores;
`options(QAST.cores = k)` sets the number of processes.

## Survival curve of the quality-adjusted time

`surv_qt_fun()` implements the estimator of Zhao and Tsiatis (1997) for the
survival curve of the quality-adjusted time: each uncensored subject is
weighted by the inverse of the Kaplan-Meier censoring survival at its
survival time, which corrects the induced informative censoring:

```{r surv-qt, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
s_qt <- surv_qt_fun(qaly = d$qt, time = d$t, status = d$status)
ord <- order(d$qt)
plot(d$qt[ord], s_qt[ord], type = "s", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Quality-adjusted survival time",
     ylab = "Estimated survival probability")
```

possible? *Scandinavian Journal of Statistics*, 42(2), 397–413.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/sjos.12112>

da Silva, A. (2026). *Regression analysis of quality-adjusted survival time
in cancer patients admitted to intensive care units: a new estimation method*.
Doctoral thesis, Institute of Mathematics and Statistics, University of São
Paulo.

Fine, J. P. and Gelber, R. D. (2001). Joint regression analysis of survival
and quality-adjusted survival. *Biometrics*, 57(2), 376–382.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00376.x>

Zhao, H. and Tsiatis, A. A. (1997). A consistent estimator for the
distribution of quality adjusted survival time. *Biometrika*, 84(2), 339–348.
<https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/84.2.339>

Zhao, H. and Tsiatis, A. A. (2000). Estimating mean quality adjusted
lifetime with censored data. *Sankhyā: The Indian Journal of Statistics,
Series B*, 62, 175–188.
